claim: EGFR signaling functions specifically in the FSCs to promote the unique partially polarized state of the FSC.
source: We found that, in the epithelial follicle stem cell (FSC) lineage of the Drosophila ovary, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling functions specifically in the FSCs to promote the unique partially polarized state of the FSC, establish apical–basal polarity throughout the lineage, and promote FSC maintenance in the niche.
evidence: Supported by mosaic analysis showing Egfr mutant FSC clones have polarity defects while prefollicle cell clones do not (Figures 3, 5, Table 1).

claim: EGFR signaling establishes apical–basal polarity throughout the FSC lineage.
source: We found that, in the epithelial follicle stem cell (FSC) lineage of the Drosophila ovary, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling functions specifically in the FSCs to promote the unique partially polarized state of the FSC, establish apical–basal polarity throughout the lineage, and promote FSC maintenance in the niche.
evidence: Demonstrated by loss of polarity markers in Egfr mutant FSC clones and their daughters (Figure 3), and by constitutive EGFR preventing apical domain formation (Figure 6).

claim: EGFR signaling promotes FSC maintenance in the niche.
source: We found that, in the epithelial follicle stem cell (FSC) lineage of the Drosophila ovary, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling functions specifically in the FSCs to promote the unique partially polarized state of the FSC, establish apical–basal polarity throughout the lineage, and promote FSC maintenance in the niche.
evidence: Supported by FSC clone frequency analysis showing rapid loss of Egfr mutant FSCs (Figure 2C) and increased competitiveness of constitutively active EGFR FSCs (Figure 2E).

claim: EGFR signals through both the Ras–Raf–MEK–Erk pathway and through the LKB1–AMPK pathway to suppress apical identity.
source: In addition, we identified a novel connection between EGFR signaling and the cell-polarity regulator liver kinase B1 (LKB1), which indicates that EGFR signals through both the Ras–Raf–MEK–Erk pathway and through the LKB1–AMPK pathway to suppress apical identity.
evidence: Supported by data showing Ras85D and lkb1 mutants phenocopy Egfr mutants (Figure 7A-E), constitutively active LKB1 rescues EgfrDN phenotype (Figure 7F-I), and EGFR is required for pAMPK (Figure 7J-K, Table 2).

claim: The development of apical–basal polarity is the earliest visible difference between FSCs and their daughters.
source: The development of apical–basal polarity is the earliest visible difference between FSCs and their daughters, and our findings demonstrate that the EGFR-mediated regulation of apical–basal polarity is essential for the segregation of stem cell and daughter cell fates.
evidence: Based on observations of polarity marker localization in FSCs versus prefollicle cells described in the Introduction and Results sections.

claim: EGFR-mediated regulation of apical–basal polarity is essential for the segregation of stem cell and daughter cell fates.
source: The development of apical–basal polarity is the earliest visible difference between FSCs and their daughters, and our findings demonstrate that the EGFR-mediated regulation of apical–basal polarity is essential for the segregation of stem cell and daughter cell fates.
evidence: Supported by data showing loss of EGFR disrupts polarity and FSC maintenance, while constitutive EGFR prevents differentiation (Figures 2-6).

claim: Two FSCs are maintained within a structure at the tip of each ovariole, called the germarium.
source: Two FSCs are maintained within a structure at the tip of each ovariole, called the germarium (Figure 1A) (Margolis and Spradling, 1995).
evidence: Cited from published literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A population of stromal escort cells located just anterior to the FSCs forms the niche, providing essential self-renewal ligands to the FSCs.
source: A population of stromal escort cells located just anterior to the FSCs forms the niche, providing essential self-renewal ligands to the FSCs (Song and Xie, 2003; Sahai-Hernandez and Nystul, 2013), and also supports early germ cell cyst development (Kirilly et al., 2011; Eliazer et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Escort cells support early germ cell cyst development.
source: A population of stromal escort cells located just anterior to the FSCs forms the niche, providing essential self-renewal ligands to the FSCs (Song and Xie, 2003; Sahai-Hernandez and Nystul, 2013), and also supports early germ cell cyst development (Kirilly et al., 2011; Eliazer et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Each FSC divides approximately once per incoming cyst.
source: As germ cell cysts mature, they move out of the escort cell region into the follicle epithelium, and each FSC divides approximately once per incoming cyst (Nystul and Spradling, 2010).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Newly produced FSC daughter cells, called prefollicle cells, move away from the niche either toward the posterior or across the germarium toward the opposite FSC niche before incorporating into the follicle epithelium.
source: Newly produced FSC daughter cells, called prefollicle cells, move away from the niche either toward the posterior or across the germarium toward the opposite FSC niche before incorporating into the follicle epithelium (Nystul and Spradling, 2007).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Bright pErk staining was detected in 90% of FSCs identified within an FSC clone.
source: Indeed, we found that bright pErk staining was detected in 90% (n = 28/31) of FSCs identified within an FSC clone, but was completely undetectable in 87% (n = 27/31) of prefollicle cells just downstream of the niche (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: pErk was completely undetectable in 87% of prefollicle cells just downstream of the niche.
source: Indeed, we found that bright pErk staining was detected in 90% (n = 28/31) of FSCs identified within an FSC clone, but was completely undetectable in 87% (n = 27/31) of prefollicle cells just downstream of the niche (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: pErk was undetectable in the FSC in 93% of Egfrf24 FSC clones.
source: Indeed, we found that pErk was undetectable in the FSC in 93% (n = 13/14) of Egfrf24 FSC clones (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1B,D.

claim: The EGFR pathway is active in FSCs and downregulated in prefollicle cells that have moved downstream from the FSC niche.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the EGFR pathway is active in FSCs and downregulated in prefollicle cells that have moved downstream from the FSC niche.
evidence: Inferred from pErk staining patterns in FSCs versus prefollicle cells (Figure 1).

claim: The frequency of mosaic ovarioles in the Egfrf24 experimental group was significantly fewer than the control group at 4, 7, and 11 dpci.
source: Nonetheless, we found significantly fewer (p < 0.02) mosaic ovarioles in the experimental group compared to the control group at all three early time points (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantified from FSC clone frequency assays shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No fully marked ovarioles were observed in the Egfrf24 experimental group at any time point (4, 7, or 11 dpci).
source: Moreover, while the frequency of fully marked ovarioles in the control group increased from 0% at 4 dpci (n = 0/157) to 10% at 11 dpci (n = 9/87), no fully marked ovarioles were observed in the experimental group at any time point (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantified from FSC clone frequency assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Egfr is required for FSC maintenance in the niche.
source: Thus, Egfr is required for FSC maintenance in the niche.
evidence: Concluded from FSC clone frequency data showing rapid loss of Egfr mutant FSCs (Figure 2C).

claim: The frequency of Egfrf24 FSC clones in the experimental group was significantly lower than that of the control group at 2 dpci.
source: We found that even at 2 dpci the frequency of Egfrf24 FSC clones in the experimental group was still significantly lower (p < 0.01) than that of the control group (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantified from FSC clone frequency assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The combined frequencies of FSC clones and prefollicle cell clones were nearly the same in the control and experimental groups at 2 dpci.
source: Therefore, we next measured the frequency of all FSC and follicle cell clones in the germarium of each ovariole at 2 dpci and found that the combined frequencies of FSC clones and prefollicle cell clones (i.e. those originating in follicle cells downstream of the FSC) were nearly the same in the control and experimental groups (Figure 2D).
evidence: Quantified from clone frequency assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The low frequency of Egfrf24 FSC clones at 2 dpci was due to a very rapid loss of Egfrf24 FSCs and not a lower rate of clone induction.
source: This suggests that the low frequency of Egfrf24 FSC clones at 2 dpci was due to a very rapid loss of Egfrf24 FSCs and not a lower rate of clone induction, as explored further in the next section.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that total clone frequencies are similar between control and experimental groups (Figure 2D).

claim: The frequency of fully marked ovarioles was significantly higher in the Egfrλtop experimental group compared to the control group at 21 dpci.
source: Whereas the frequency and distribution of FSC clones was similar in both groups at 7 dpci (p > 0.33), the frequency of fully marked ovarioles was significantly higher in the experimental group compared to the control group at 21 dpci (18% in wildtype vs 31% in Egfrλtop, p < 0.02) (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantified from FSC clone frequency assays shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: FSCs and prefollicle cells with constitutively active EGFR signaling are hypercompetitive for the niche relative to the wildtype FSCs in the same tissue.
source: This indicates that FSCs and prefollicle cells with constitutively active EGFR signaling are hypercompetitive for the niche relative to the wildtype FSCs in the same tissue.
evidence: Inferred from the increased frequency of fully marked ovarioles in Egfrλtop experimental group (Figure 2E).

claim: All Egfrf24 FSC clones had severe morphological defects that suggested a loss of cell polarity.
source: Interestingly, all Egfrf24 FSC clones and a subset of early Egfrf24 prefollicle cell clones had severe morphological defects that suggested a loss of cell polarity.
evidence: Observed in microscopy images of Egfrf24 FSC clones (Figure 2B).

claim: A subset of early Egfrf24 prefollicle cell clones had severe morphological defects that suggested a loss of cell polarity.
source: Interestingly, all Egfrf24 FSC clones and a subset of early Egfrf24 prefollicle cell clones had severe morphological defects that suggested a loss of cell polarity.
evidence: Observed in microscopy images and quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: The Egfrf24 cells in FSC clones failed to incorporate into the follicle epithelium and did not encapsulate germ cell cysts.
source: Indeed, the Egfrf24 cells in these clones failed to incorporate into the follicle epithelium and did not encapsulate germ cell cysts (Figure 2B).
evidence: Observed in microscopy images shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The lateral marker Dlg was undetectable on the cell membranes in 100% of Egfrf24 FSC clones.
source: We found that the lateral Dlg was undetectable on the cell membranes in 100% (n = 38/38) of Egfrf24 FSC clones (Figure 3F and Table 1).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 3F and Table 1.

claim: The apical marker aPKC was undetectable in all Egfrf24 FSC clones.
source: In addition, we found that the apical marker aPKC, the apical–lateral marker Baz, and the adherens junction component DE-cadherin (DE-cad) were also undetectable in all Egfrf24 FSC clones (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The apical–lateral marker Baz was undetectable in all Egfrf24 FSC clones.
source: In addition, we found that the apical marker aPKC, the apical–lateral marker Baz, and the adherens junction component DE-cadherin (DE-cad) were also undetectable in all Egfrf24 FSC clones (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The adherens junction component DE-cadherin (DE-cad) was undetectable in all Egfrf24 FSC clones.
source: In addition, we found that the apical marker aPKC, the apical–lateral marker Baz, and the adherens junction component DE-cadherin (DE-cad) were also undetectable in all Egfrf24 FSC clones (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The basal marker β-integrin was detectable in the cytoplasm but not on the cell membrane in all Egfrf24 FSC clones.
source: Moreover, the basal marker β-integrin was detectable in the cytoplasm but not on the cell membrane in all Egfrf24 FSC clones (Figure 3J).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Polarity was not disrupted in 96% of negatively marked wildtype FSC clones.
source: In contrast, polarity was not disrupted in 96% (n = 103/107) of negatively marked wildtype FSC clones (Figure 3A–E and Table 1), and we consistently found that all of these cell-polarity markers were properly localized on the cell membranes of Egfr+/f24 follicle cells in germaria with Egfrf24 clones (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 3A–E and Table 1.

claim: All cell-polarity markers were properly localized on the cell membranes of Egfr+/f24 follicle cells in germaria with Egfrf24 clones.
source: In contrast, polarity was not disrupted in 96% (n = 103/107) of negatively marked wildtype FSC clones (Figure 3A–E and Table 1), and we consistently found that all of these cell-polarity markers were properly localized on the cell membranes of Egfr+/f24 follicle cells in germaria with Egfrf24 clones (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 3F–J.

claim: 94% of positively marked Egfrf2 FSC clones had an identical phenotype as negatively marked Egfrf24 FSC clones.
source: In addition, using the MARCM system we generated positively marked FSC clones homozygous for another loss of function allele, Egfrf2, and found that 94% (n = 17/18) had an identical phenotype as negatively marked Egfrf24 FSC clones, while polarity was not disrupted in 99% (n = 83/84) of positively marked wildtype FSC clones (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Polarity was not disrupted in 99% of positively marked wildtype FSC clones.
source: In addition, using the MARCM system we generated positively marked FSC clones homozygous for another loss of function allele, Egfrf2, and found that 94% (n = 17/18) had an identical phenotype as negatively marked Egfrf24 FSC clones, while polarity was not disrupted in 99% (n = 83/84) of positively marked wildtype FSC clones (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of a dominant-negative allele of Egfr (EgfrDN) using a follicle cell-specific driver 109-30-Gal4 phenocopied the polarity defects observed in Egfrf24 clones, albeit with a lower penetrance (46% of germaria).
source: Lastly, we found that expression of a dominant-negative allele of Egfr (EgfrDN) using a follicle cell-specific driver 109-30-Gal4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) (Hartman et al., 2010) phenocopied the polarity defects we observed in Egfrf24 clones, albeit with a lower penetrance (46% of germaria, n = 118/255, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C.

claim: The loss of cell polarity in Egfrf24 and Egfrf2 FSC clones is cell autonomous.
source: Together, these controls verify that the phenotypes we observed are not due to the genetic background, that they are not an artifact of the dissection process (Haack et al., 2013), and that the loss of cell polarity in Egfrf24 and Egfrf2 FSC clones is cell autonomous.
evidence: Inferred from multiple control experiments including MARCM clones and EgfrDN expression (Figure 3 and supplements).

claim: FasIII was consistently detectable on the cell membrane in Egfrf24 FSC clones.
source: To determine whether Egfrf24 FSC clones retained other markers of epithelial identity we stained for FasIII, which is commonly used to identify follicle cells, and found that it was consistently detectable on the cell membrane (Figure 4A).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Traffic jam was unaffected in Egfrf24 FSC clones.
source: Likewise, we found that Traffic jam, a transcription factor that is specific for somatic cells that contact the germline (Li et al., 2003), was also unaffected (Figure 4A).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The frequency of Egfrf24 FSC clones with Cas3+ follicle cells in the germarium (17%) was comparable to the frequency observed in the sibling controls (15%).
source: We found that while all Egfrf24 FSC clones had polarity defects, the frequency of Egfrf24 FSC clones with Cas3+ follicle cells in the germarium (17%, n = 3/16) was comparable to the frequency observed in the sibling controls (15%, n = 6/41, Figure 4C).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The polarity defect in Egfrf24 FSC clones is not likely to be due to a loss of follicle cell identity or the induction of apoptosis.
source: Thus, the polarity defect in Egfrf24 FSC clones is not likely to be due to a loss of follicle cell identity or the induction of apoptosis.
evidence: Inferred from observations that FasIII and Traffic jam are normal and Cas3 frequency is not elevated in Egfrf24 FSC clones (Figure 4).

claim: Dlg was not disrupted in 94% of Egfrf24 prefollicle cell clones.
source: Although nearly all Egfrf24 and Egfrf2 FSC clones had polarity defects, Dlg was not disrupted in 94% (n = 82/87) and 95% (n = 121/127) of Egfrf24 and Egfrf2 prefollicle cell clones, respectively (Table 1, Figure 5F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2; see 'Materials and methods' for a description of FSC clones vs prefollicle cell clones).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Table 1, Figure 5F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dlg was not disrupted in 95% of Egfrf2 prefollicle cell clones.
source: Although nearly all Egfrf24 and Egfrf2 FSC clones had polarity defects, Dlg was not disrupted in 94% (n = 82/87) and 95% (n = 121/127) of Egfrf24 and Egfrf2 prefollicle cell clones, respectively (Table 1, Figure 5F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2; see 'Materials and methods' for a description of FSC clones vs prefollicle cell clones).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Table 1, Figure 5F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: aPKC, Baz, DE-cad, and β-integrin were not substantially disrupted in large wildtype and Egfrf24 prefollicle cell clones.
source: In addition, aPKC, Baz, DE-cad, and β-integrin were not substantially disrupted in large wildtype and Egfrf24 prefollicle cell clones (Figure 5).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: pErk was undetectable in nearly all Egfrf24 prefollicle cell clones.
source: Lastly, we found that pErk was undetectable in nearly all Egfrf24 prefollicle cell clones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), verifying that the lack of polarity defects in these clones was not due to a perdurance of EGFR signaling.
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: EGFR is not needed for the continued establishment or maintenance of cell polarity in follicle cells downstream of the FSC.
source: Together these data indicate that EGFR is not needed for the continued establishment or maintenance of cell polarity in follicle cells downstream of the FSC.
evidence: Inferred from observations that Egfr mutant prefollicle cell clones have normal polarity (Figure 5, Table 1).

claim: 15% of Egfrf24 clones in the germarium at 2 dpci that did not include a cell in the FSC niche had polarity defects identical to those of Egfrf24 FSC clones.
source: At 2 dpci, 15% (n = 13/84, Figure 2D) of Egfrf24 clones in the germarium that did not include a cell in the FSC niche (Figure 2F) had polarity defects identical to those of Egfrf24 FSC clones.
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2F.

claim: Polarity-defective prefollicle cell clones at 2 dpci likely originated from a recently replaced FSC.
source: Since Egfrf24 FSCs are rapidly lost from the niche, it is likely that these polarity-defective prefollicle cell clones originated from a recently replaced FSC, but had not yet moved out of the germarium at this early time point.
evidence: Inferred from the rapid loss of Egfr mutant FSCs and the timing of clone observation.

claim: The cell polarity defects in Egfrf24 FSC clones arise within 2 dpci.
source: These observations are consistent with a very rapid loss of Egfrf24 FSCs from the niche and demonstrate that the cell polarity defects arise within 2 dpci.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of polarity-defective prefollicle cell clones at 2 dpci (Figure 2D, 2F).

claim: Egfr is required specifically in FSCs to establish cell polarity throughout the FSC lineage.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that Egfr is required specifically in FSCs to establish cell polarity throughout the FSC lineage.
evidence: Concluded from observations that Egfr mutant FSC clones have polarity defects while prefollicle cell clones do not (Figures 3, 5, Table 1).

claim: 21% of germaria with constitutively active EGFR signaling were elongated and completely lacked a Region 3 cyst.
source: We found that Region 3 cysts were always present in germaria from control flies, but that 21% (n = 25/119) of the germaria with constitutively active EGFR signaling were elongated and completely lacked a Region 3 cyst (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Quantified from microscopy observations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In 70% of germaria with constitutively active EGFR signaling that had Region 3 cysts, aPKC was delocalized from the cell surface of follicle cells surrounding these cysts.
source: In nearly all of the remaining germaria (70%, n = 83/119), Region 3 cysts were present but aPKC was delocalized from the cell surface of follicle cells surrounding these cysts (Figure 6B,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 6B,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Many of the follicle cells in Region 3 with constitutively active EGFR signaling had a more pointed shape that resembled FSCs or early prefollicle cells.
source: In addition, many of the follicle cells in this region were not cuboidal but instead had a more pointed shape that resembled FSCs or early prefollicle cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Observed in microscopy images shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Dlg was still detectable on the cell membranes of follicle cells with constitutively active EGFR signaling.
source: Interestingly, Dlg was still detectable on the cell membranes of follicle cells with constitutively active EGFR signaling (Figure 6B,D), indicating that lateral identity was largely unaffected in these cells.
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: Bright puncta of Baz staining were still visible on the cell membrane near sites of contact with the germline in 76% of germaria with constitutively active EGFR signaling.
source: In addition, bright puncta of Baz staining were still visible on the cell membrane near sites of contact with the germline in 76% (n = 86/110) of these germaria, suggesting that apical–lateral identity is also largely unaffected (Figure 6C–D,F).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 6C–D,F.

claim: Downregulation of EGFR signaling is required for the formation of apical domains in prefollicle cells.
source: Therefore, downregulation of EGFR signaling is required for the formation of apical domains in prefollicle cells.
evidence: Concluded from observations that constitutively active EGFR prevents aPKC localization to apical surfaces (Figure 6).

claim: 48% of Ras85D− FSC clones lacked Dlg on the cell surface and had the same morphological defects as Egfrf24 FSC clones.
source: Specifically, we found that 48% (n = 15/31) of Ras85D− FSC clones lacked Dlg on the cell surface and had the same morphological defects as Egfrf24 FSC clones, whereas 96% (n = 45/47) of large Ras85D− prefollicle cell clones had a normal cell shape and properly localized Dlg to the cell membrane (Figure 7B,E).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 7B,E.

claim: 96% of large Ras85D− prefollicle cell clones had a normal cell shape and properly localized Dlg to the cell membrane.
source: Specifically, we found that 48% (n = 15/31) of Ras85D− FSC clones lacked Dlg on the cell surface and had the same morphological defects as Egfrf24 FSC clones, whereas 96% (n = 45/47) of large Ras85D− prefollicle cell clones had a normal cell shape and properly localized Dlg to the cell membrane (Figure 7B,E).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 7B,E.

claim: Cell polarity was disrupted in 46% of FSC clones that were homozygous for lkb1−.
source: First, we found that cell polarity was disrupted in 46% (n = 17/37) of FSC clones that were homozygous for lkb1[4A4−2], a deletion allele that is predicted to be a null (Martin and St Johnston, 2003) (here referred to as lkb1−), whereas polarity was not disrupted in 93% (n = 62/67) of lkb1− prefollicle cell clones (Figure 7C–E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 7C–E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Polarity was not disrupted in 93% of lkb1− prefollicle cell clones.
source: First, we found that cell polarity was disrupted in 46% (n = 17/37) of FSC clones that were homozygous for lkb1[4A4−2], a deletion allele that is predicted to be a null (Martin and St Johnston, 2003) (here referred to as lkb1−), whereas polarity was not disrupted in 93% (n = 62/67) of lkb1− prefollicle cell clones (Figure 7C–E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 7C–E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: pAMPK was detectable in follicle cells of 59% of wildtype germaria.
source: Therefore, we stained for phosphorylated AMPK (pAMPK) and found that it was detectable in follicle cells of 59% (n = 95/160) of wildtype germaria (Table 2).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Table 2.

claim: pAMPK signal was absent in 100% of lkb1− FSC clones.
source: We found that, whereas pAMPK signal was absent in 100% (n = 57/57) of lkb1− FSC clones, it was clearly detectable in the wildtype (lkb1+/−) follicle cells in 68% (n = 39/57) of these same germaria (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: pAMPK was clearly detectable in the wildtype (lkb1+/−) follicle cells in 68% of germaria with lkb1− FSC clones.
source: We found that, whereas pAMPK signal was absent in 100% (n = 57/57) of lkb1− FSC clones, it was clearly detectable in the wildtype (lkb1+/−) follicle cells in 68% (n = 39/57) of these same germaria (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: The LKB1–AMPK pathway is active in follicle cells within the germarium.
source: These data confirm that the LKB1–AMPK pathway is active in follicle cells within the germarium, and that LKB1 promotes the establishment of follicle cell polarity.
evidence: Concluded from pAMPK staining in wildtype follicle cells and its absence in lkb1− clones (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E, Table 2).

claim: LKB1 promotes the establishment of follicle cell polarity.
source: These data confirm that the LKB1–AMPK pathway is active in follicle cells within the germarium, and that LKB1 promotes the establishment of follicle cell polarity.
evidence: Concluded from observations that lkb1− FSC clones have polarity defects (Figure 7C–E).

claim: Co-expression of lkb1S535E with EgfrDN produced an approximately threefold reduction in the percentage of germaria with follicle cell polarity defects (14%).
source: We found that co-expression of lkb1S535E with EgfrDN produced an approximately threefold reduction in the percentage of germaria with follicle cell polarity defects (14%, n = 21/154, Figure 7F–I), indicating that constitutive activation of LKB1 partially rescued the Egfr mutant polarity defect.
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 7F–I.

claim: Constitutive activation of LKB1 partially rescued the Egfr mutant polarity defect.
source: We found that co-expression of lkb1S535E with EgfrDN produced an approximately threefold reduction in the percentage of germaria with follicle cell polarity defects (14%, n = 21/154, Figure 7F–I), indicating that constitutive activation of LKB1 partially rescued the Egfr mutant polarity defect.
evidence: Concluded from the reduction in polarity defects when lkb1S535E is co-expressed with EgfrDN (Figure 7F–I).

claim: There was a 29% decrease in germaria with detectable pAMPK when expressing EgfrDN (42%).
source: We observed a 29% decrease in germaria with detectable pAMPK (42%, n = 28/66, Table 2) and found a strong correlation between the absence of pAMPK signal and the absence of Dlg on the cell membranes in germaria expressing EgfrDN (Figure 7K and Table 2, p < 10−4).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 7K and Table 2.

claim: There is a strong correlation between the absence of pAMPK signal and the absence of Dlg on the cell membranes in germaria expressing EgfrDN.
source: We observed a 29% decrease in germaria with detectable pAMPK (42%, n = 28/66, Table 2) and found a strong correlation between the absence of pAMPK signal and the absence of Dlg on the cell membranes in germaria expressing EgfrDN (Figure 7K and Table 2, p < 10−4).
evidence: Statistical analysis of immunostaining data shown in Figure 7K and Table 2.

claim: EGFR functions through both the canonical Ras–Raf–MEK–Erk pathway and the LKB1–AMPK pathway to establish epithelial polarity in the FSC.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that EGFR functions through both the canonical Ras–Raf–MEK–Erk pathway and the LKB1–AMPK pathway to establish epithelial polarity in the FSC.
evidence: Concluded from genetic experiments showing Ras85D and lkb1 mutants phenocopy Egfr mutants, and EGFR is required for pAMPK (Figure 7).

claim: EGFR signaling is required in an epithelial stem cell population, but not in its daughter cells, to facilitate the development of apical–basal polarity throughout the lineage.
source: In this study, we found that EGFR signaling is required in an epithelial stem cell population, but not in its daughter cells, to facilitate the development of apical–basal polarity throughout the lineage.
evidence: Summarizes findings from Figures 1-5 showing EGFR is required in FSCs but not prefollicle cells for polarity.

claim: EGFR signaling is active specifically in FSCs.
source: Our finding that EGFR signaling is active specifically in FSCs is supported by our stains for pErk (which we detected specifically in FSCs) and by our mosaic analysis (which indicated that deletion of Egfr from FSCs produces a cell-polarity phenotype, whereas deletion of Egfr from the immediate daughter cells does not).
evidence: Supported by pErk staining (Figure 1) and mosaic analysis (Figures 3, 5).

claim: Loss of Egfr from FSCs disrupts the basal and lateral domains of the FSCs (as well as their daughters).
source: In our subsequent analysis, we found that loss of Egfr from FSCs disrupts the basal and lateral domains of the FSCs (as well as their daughters), whereas constitutive activation of Egfr is sufficient to suppress the formation of the apical domains in prefollicle cells.
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments showing loss of Dlg and β-integrin in Egfr mutant FSC clones (Figure 3).

claim: Constitutive activation of Egfr is sufficient to suppress the formation of the apical domains in prefollicle cells.
source: In our subsequent analysis, we found that loss of Egfr from FSCs disrupts the basal and lateral domains of the FSCs (as well as their daughters), whereas constitutive activation of Egfr is sufficient to suppress the formation of the apical domains in prefollicle cells.
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments showing delocalized aPKC in germaria expressing Egfrλtop (Figure 6).

claim: EGFR signaling promotes basal and lateral identity and suppresses apical identity in FSCs.
source: Collectively these observations support a model (Figure 8) in which EGFR signaling promotes basal and lateral identity and suppresses apical identity in FSCs.
evidence: Model based on observations from loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments (Figures 3, 6).

claim: Despite the importance of EGFR signaling in FSCs, Egfr is dispensable for the maintenance and continued development of cell polarity in prefollicle cells.
source: It is interesting that, despite the importance of EGFR signaling in FSCs, Egfr is dispensable for the maintenance and continued development of cell polarity in prefollicle cells (Figure 5).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments showing normal polarity in Egfr mutant prefollicle cell clones (Figure 5).

claim: In polarized epithelial cells, apical and lateral identities are maintained by a process of mutual exclusion in which the cortical localization of the Par-6/aPKC complex is suppressed by Lgl and vice versa.
source: In polarized epithelial cells, apical and lateral identities are maintained by a process of mutual exclusion in which the cortical localization of the Par-6/aPKC complex is suppressed by Lgl and vice versa (Hutterer et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: The reactivation of EGFR signaling in follicle cells during mid- and late-oogenesis does not seem to disrupt polarity.
source: Indeed, the reactivation of EGFR signaling in follicle cells during mid- and late-oogenesis does not seem to disrupt polarity, suggesting that the influence of EGFR signaling on cell polarity is diminished in these stages when the cells are more differentiated and fully polarized.
evidence: Inferred from observations of pErk in mid-stage follicles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) without apparent polarity defects.

claim: Prefollicle cells produced by FSCs that are mutant for Egfr exhibit cell-polarity defects.
source: This mutual dependency may also explain why prefollicle cells produced by FSCs that are mutant for Egfr exhibit cell-polarity defects (Figure 3).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments showing polarity defects in daughters of Egfr mutant FSCs (Figure 3).

claim: Egfr− FSCs lack basal and lateral domain identities.
source: Since Egfr− FSCs lack basal and lateral domain identities, they may be unable to contribute polarity information to their prefollicle cell daughters, leaving these cells with no polarity cues to build upon and therefore rendering them incapable of specifying basal, lateral or apical domains.
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments showing loss of Dlg and β-integrin in Egfr mutant FSCs (Figure 3).

claim: Loss of lkb1 phenocopies loss of Egfr.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that EGFR signaling regulates cell polarity in part by activating LKB1. First, our observations that loss of lkb1 phenocopies loss of Egfr, and that constitutively active LKB1 partially rescues the phenotypes caused by a decrease in Egfr function, indicate that EGFR and LKB1 operate together to promote cell polarity in the FSC lineage.
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments showing similar polarity defects in lkb1 and Egfr mutant FSC clones (Figure 7).

claim: Constitutively active LKB1 partially rescues the phenotypes caused by a decrease in Egfr function.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that EGFR signaling regulates cell polarity in part by activating LKB1. First, our observations that loss of lkb1 phenocopies loss of Egfr, and that constitutively active LKB1 partially rescues the phenotypes caused by a decrease in Egfr function, indicate that EGFR and LKB1 operate together to promote cell polarity in the FSC lineage.
evidence: Observed in rescue experiments showing reduced polarity defects when lkb1S535E is co-expressed with EgfrDN (Figure 7F-I).

claim: EGFR and LKB1 operate together to promote cell polarity in the FSC lineage.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that EGFR signaling regulates cell polarity in part by activating LKB1. First, our observations that loss of lkb1 phenocopies loss of Egfr, and that constitutively active LKB1 partially rescues the phenotypes caused by a decrease in Egfr function, indicate that EGFR and LKB1 operate together to promote cell polarity in the FSC lineage.
evidence: Concluded from genetic interaction experiments (Figure 7).

claim: The LKB1-dependent phosphorylation of AMPK is dependent in part on Egfr.
source: Second, our observation that the LKB1-dependent phosphorylation of AMPK is dependent in part on Egfr suggests that LKB1 is activated by EGFR signaling.
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments showing reduced pAMPK in EgfrDN-expressing germaria (Figure 7J-K, Table 2).

claim: LKB1 is activated by EGFR signaling.
source: Second, our observation that the LKB1-dependent phosphorylation of AMPK is dependent in part on Egfr suggests that LKB1 is activated by EGFR signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pAMPK is reduced when EGFR is inhibited (Figure 7J-K, Table 2).

claim: LKB1 is a 'master regulator' of cell polarity.
source: LKB1 is a 'master regulator' of cell polarity (Partanen et al., 2013), capable of initiating apical–basal polarity even in cultured cells that lack cell–cell contacts (Baas et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: LKB1 is capable of initiating apical–basal polarity even in cultured cells that lack cell–cell contacts.
source: LKB1 is a 'master regulator' of cell polarity (Partanen et al., 2013), capable of initiating apical–basal polarity even in cultured cells that lack cell–cell contacts (Baas et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: In Drosophila, LKB1 is required in follicle cells to prevent apical proteins from encroaching into the lateral domain.
source: In Drosophila, LKB1 is required in follicle cells to prevent apical proteins from encroaching into the lateral domain (Martin and St Johnston, 2003).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: EGFR promotes apical constriction of epithelial cells in the tracheal placode during Drosophila development.
source: Moreover, although the intermediate steps were not investigated, a recent study demonstrated that EGFR promotes apical constriction of epithelial cells in the tracheal placode during Drosophila development (Kondo and Hayashi, 2013).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: In many Drosophila cell types, EGFR signaling operates exclusively through the linear Ras–Raf–MEK–Erk cascade.
source: In many Drosophila cell types, EGFR signaling operates exclusively through the linear Ras–Raf–MEK–Erk cascade (Perrimon et al., 2012; Shilo, 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: The loss of Ras85D produces a substantially less penetrant phenotype than loss of Egfr.
source: However, our finding that the loss of Ras85D produces a substantially less penetrant phenotype than loss of Egfr (Figure 7E) suggests that the pathway bifurcates upstream of Ras85D, placing lkb1 in a separate pathway downstream of EGFR.
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The EGFR pathway bifurcates upstream of Ras85D, placing lkb1 in a separate pathway downstream of EGFR.
source: However, our finding that the loss of Ras85D produces a substantially less penetrant phenotype than loss of Egfr (Figure 7E) suggests that the pathway bifurcates upstream of Ras85D, placing lkb1 in a separate pathway downstream of EGFR.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in penetrance between Ras85D and Egfr mutants (Figure 7E).

claim: EGFR can activate PKA in a Ras-independent manner in the adult Drosophila brain.
source: Consistent with this possibility, a study of the adult Drosophila brain found that EGFR can activate PKA in a Ras-independent manner (Hannan et al., 2006), and PKA is a well-established activator of LKB1 (Collins et al., 2000; Sapkota et al., 2001).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: PKA is a well-established activator of LKB1.
source: Consistent with this possibility, a study of the adult Drosophila brain found that EGFR can activate PKA in a Ras-independent manner (Hannan et al., 2006), and PKA is a well-established activator of LKB1 (Collins et al., 2000; Sapkota et al., 2001).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Each of the individual steps of the pathway from EGFR through to PKA, LKB1, and AMPK to apical–basal polarity have been observed in studies of mammalian tissues.
source: Moreover, each of the individual steps of this pathway from EGFR through to PKA, LKB1, and AMPK to apical–basal polarity have been observed in studies of mammalian tissues (Collins et al., 2000; Tortora and Ciardiello, 2002; Xie et al., 2006; Shackelford and Shaw, 2009), suggesting that these connections make up an evolutionarily conserved pathway.
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: The EGFR-PKA-LKB1-AMPK pathway to apical–basal polarity is evolutionarily conserved.
source: Moreover, each of the individual steps of this pathway from EGFR through to PKA, LKB1, and AMPK to apical–basal polarity have been observed in studies of mammalian tissues (Collins et al., 2000; Tortora and Ciardiello, 2002; Xie et al., 2006; Shackelford and Shaw, 2009), suggesting that these connections make up an evolutionarily conserved pathway.
evidence: Inferred from observations in both Drosophila and mammalian systems cited in the literature.

claim: EGFR signaling regulates the segregation of stem cell and daughter cell fates in the FSC lineage.
source: In addition to promoting apical–basal polarity, our findings indicate that EGFR signaling also regulates the segregation of stem cell and daughter cell fates in the FSC lineage.
evidence: Concluded from FSC maintenance and competition assays (Figure 2).

claim: EGFR is required for the FSC fate.
source: Specifically, our finding that Egfrf24 FSC clones are rapidly lost from the tissue indicates that EGFR is required for the FSC fate; whereas our observation that constitutively active EGFR signaling causes prefollicle cells to retain an FSC-like morphology and replace wildtype stem cells more often suggests that EGFR signaling must be downregulated to permit differentiation.
evidence: Concluded from FSC clone frequency data showing rapid loss of Egfr mutant FSCs (Figure 2C).

claim: EGFR signaling must be downregulated to permit differentiation.
source: Specifically, our finding that Egfrf24 FSC clones are rapidly lost from the tissue indicates that EGFR is required for the FSC fate; whereas our observation that constitutively active EGFR signaling causes prefollicle cells to retain an FSC-like morphology and replace wildtype stem cells more often suggests that EGFR signaling must be downregulated to permit differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from observations that constitutively active EGFR prevents apical domain formation and increases FSC competitiveness (Figures 2E, 6).

claim: The activation of the canonical EGFR pathway leading to the phosphorylation of Erk is likely to directly regulate the activity of many genes in the FSC self-renewal program.
source: First, the activation of the canonical EGFR pathway leading to the phosphorylation of Erk is likely to directly regulate the activity of many genes in the FSC self-renewal program.
evidence: Based on known functions of the EGFR-Erk pathway and detection of pErk in FSCs (Figure 1).

claim: EGFR signaling may interact with other pathways, such as the Wingless pathway, that are required for FSC self-renewal.
source: Second, EGFR signaling may interact with other pathways, such as the Wingless pathway, that are required for FSC self-renewal (Song and Xie, 2003; Sahai-Hernandez and Nystul, 2013).
evidence: Speculated based on known requirement of Wingless for FSC self-renewal and examples of EGFR-Wingless crosstalk in other tissues.

claim: EGFR and Wingless signaling cooperate to specify cell fate in the Drosophila wing disc.
source: Indeed, EGFR and Wingless signaling cooperate to specify cell fate in other Drosophila tissues such as the wing disc (Szüts et al., 1997) and the intestinal epithelium (Xu et al., 2011), and thus there may be similar cross-talk in the FSC niche compartment.
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: EGFR and Wingless signaling cooperate to specify cell fate in the Drosophila intestinal epithelium.
source: Indeed, EGFR and Wingless signaling cooperate to specify cell fate in other Drosophila tissues such as the wing disc (Szüts et al., 1997) and the intestinal epithelium (Xu et al., 2011), and thus there may be similar cross-talk in the FSC niche compartment.
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: There may be similar cross-talk between EGFR and Wingless signaling in the FSC niche compartment.
source: Indeed, EGFR and Wingless signaling cooperate to specify cell fate in other Drosophila tissues such as the wing disc (Szüts et al., 1997) and the intestinal epithelium (Xu et al., 2011), and thus there may be similar cross-talk in the FSC niche compartment.
evidence: Speculated based on observations in other Drosophila tissues.

claim: EGFR signaling is required for FSC maintenance in the niche in part because of its role in regulating cell polarity.
source: Third, our data strongly suggest that EGFR signaling is required for FSC maintenance in the niche in part because of its role in regulating cell polarity.
evidence: Inferred from observations that EGFR regulates both polarity and FSC maintenance (Figures 2-3).

claim: EGFR signaling is required for the formation of the cellular junctions that are known to anchor FSCs in the niche.
source: Specifically, our observation that DE-cad and β-integrin are absent from the membranes of cells in Egfrf24 FSC clones indicates that EGFR signaling is required for the formation of the cellular junctions that are known to anchor FSCs in the niche (Song and Xie, 2002; O'Reilly et al., 2008).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments showing loss of DE-cad and β-integrin in Egfr mutant FSC clones (Figure 3I-J), and cited literature on FSC anchoring.

claim: The lack of polarity in Egfrf24 FSCs could affect other processes, such as cellular trafficking, cell division, and signal transduction that may be important for the self-renewal program.
source: In addition, the lack of polarity in Egfrf24 FSCs could also affect other processes, such as cellular trafficking, cell division, and signal transduction that may be important for the self-renewal program.
evidence: Speculated based on known roles of cell polarity in various cellular processes.

claim: EGFR signaling, and the role that the pathway plays in regulating cell polarity, are an essential part of the program that promotes the segregation of FSC and daughter cell fates.
source: Collectively these studies demonstrate that EGFR signaling, and the role that the pathway plays in regulating cell polarity, are an essential part of the program that promotes the segregation of FSC and daughter cell fates.
evidence: Concluded from all experimental findings showing EGFR regulates both polarity and FSC fate (Figures 1-7).

claim: EGFR signaling is known to promote a stem-like or less differentiated state in other epithelial tissues.
source: EGFR signaling is known to promote a stem-like or less differentiated state in other epithelial tissues as well.
evidence: General statement supported by examples from interfollicular epidermis and intestinal epithelium cited below.

claim: EGFR signaling induces proliferation of progenitor cells in the basal layer of the interfollicular epidermis, and is downregulated in cells within the suprabasal layers that are differentiating into mature keratinocytes.
source: For example, EGFR signaling induces proliferation of progenitor cells in the basal layer of the interfollicular epidermis, and is downregulated in cells within the suprabasal layers that are differentiating into mature keratinocytes (Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: EGFR signaling is required for the maintenance and proliferation of the stem cells in the Drosophila intestinal epithelium.
source: Likewise, EGFR signaling is required for the maintenance and proliferation of the stem cells in the Drosophila intestinal epithelium (Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: EGFR signaling is commonly upregulated in epithelial cancers, such as triple negative breast cancer, that have a stem cell-like molecular profile.
source: Moreover, EGFR signaling is commonly upregulated in epithelial cancers, such as triple negative breast cancer, that have a stem cell-like molecular profile.
evidence: General knowledge about EGFR in cancer biology.

claim: The specific effects of EGFR signaling in the stem cells of other epithelial tissues are not well understood.
source: However, the specific effects of EGFR signaling in the stem cells of these tissues are not well understood.
evidence: General statement about gaps in current knowledge.

claim: EGFR signaling can promote a loss of cell polarity in differentiated epithelial cells by contributing to the activation of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.
source: In addition, although EGFR signaling can promote a loss of cell polarity in differentiated epithelial cells by contributing to the activation of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, it is unclear whether or how this function of EGFR signaling relates to cell fate specification.
evidence: General knowledge about EGFR's role in EMT.

claim: It is unclear whether or how EGFR's function in promoting loss of cell polarity in differentiated epithelial cells relates to cell fate specification.
source: In addition, although EGFR signaling can promote a loss of cell polarity in differentiated epithelial cells by contributing to the activation of the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, it is unclear whether or how this function of EGFR signaling relates to cell fate specification.
evidence: Statement about gaps in current understanding.

claim: EGFR signaling promotes the stem cell fate at least in part by specifying the unique polarity of the stem cell.
source: Our study suggests that EGFR signaling promotes the stem cell fate at least in part by specifying the unique polarity of the stem cell.
evidence: Concluded from findings showing EGFR regulates both polarity and FSC fate (Figures 1-7).

claim: The regulation of cell polarity may be a common mechanism by which cell fates are specified in other epithelial tissues.
source: It will be interesting to determine whether the regulation of cell polarity is a common mechanism by which cell fates are specified in other epithelial tissues as well.
evidence: Speculated based on findings in FSCs and potential broader implications.

claim: The FSCs have a lateral domain (which includes Discs large (Dlg), Lethal giant larvae (Lgl), and Scribble), a basal domain (defined by the localization of integrins to the surface that contacts the basement membrane), but no discrete apical domain.
source: The FSCs have a lateral domain (which includes Discs large (Dlg), Lethal giant larvae (Lgl), and Scribble), a basal domain (defined by the localization of integrins to the surface that contacts the basement membrane), but no discrete apical domain.
evidence: Described based on observations of polarity marker localization in FSCs.

claim: In FSCs, apical determinants are either undetectable or diffusely localized throughout the FSCs.
source: Instead, apical determinants are either undetectable or diffusely localized throughout the FSCs.
evidence: Described based on observations of apical marker localization in FSCs.

claim: Nascent apical domains are visible in adjacent, differentiating prefollicle cells.
source: In contrast, nascent apical domains are visible in adjacent, differentiating prefollicle cells.
evidence: Described based on observations of apical marker localization in prefollicle cells.

claim: Bazooka (Baz, the Drosophila homolog of Par-3) is the first marker to become visible on the cell membrane in prefollicle cells.
source: The apical–lateral determinant, Bazooka (Baz, the Drosophila homolog of Par-3), is the first marker to become visible on the cell membrane, followed by atypical protein kinase C (aPKC), which localizes to the apical surface and positions Baz at the apical–lateral junctions.
evidence: Described based on observations of polarity marker localization during follicle cell differentiation.

claim: Atypical protein kinase C (aPKC) localizes to the apical surface and positions Baz at the apical–lateral junctions in prefollicle cells.
source: The apical–lateral determinant, Bazooka (Baz, the Drosophila homolog of Par-3), is the first marker to become visible on the cell membrane, followed by atypical protein kinase C (aPKC), which localizes to the apical surface and positions Baz at the apical–lateral junctions.
evidence: Described based on observations of polarity marker localization during follicle cell differentiation.

claim: Proteins in the Crumbs complex colocalize with aPKC and reinforce the apical identity in prefollicle cells.
source: Further downstream, proteins in the Crumbs complex colocalize with aPKC and reinforce the apical identity.
evidence: Described based on known functions of the Crumbs complex in establishing apical polarity.

claim: Adherens junctions relocalize during follicle cell differentiation from a broad band along the anterior lateral surface of FSCs to discrete puncta at the apical–lateral junctions in differentiated follicle cells.
source: Adherens junctions also relocalize during follicle cell differentiation from a broad band along the anterior lateral surface of FSCs to discrete puncta at the apical–lateral junctions in differentiated follicle cells.
evidence: Described based on observations of adherens junction marker localization during follicle cell differentiation.

claim: Once cell polarity is established in epithelial tissues, it is maintained through a highly conserved, self-sustaining process of mutual repression between the apical and lateral protein complexes.
source: Once cell polarity is established in epithelial tissues, it is maintained through a highly conserved, self-sustaining process of mutual repression between the apical and lateral protein complexes (Betschinger et al., 2003; Bilder et al., 2003; Tanentzapf and Tepass, 2003).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Since apical and lateral complexes are absent or immature during the establishment of cell polarity, additional signals are required at earlier stages.
source: However, since these complexes are absent or immature during the establishment of cell polarity, additional signals are required at earlier stages.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutual repression requires both complexes to be present.

claim: Liver kinase B1 (LKB1) regulates multiple proteins involved in the establishment of cell polarity, including AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK).
source: One such signal is provided by liver kinase B1 (LKB1), which regulates multiple proteins involved in the establishment of cell polarity, including AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Nakano and Takashima, 2012).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: LKB1 is activated by protein kinase A (PKA) and Par-1, and is required for follicle cell polarity.
source: LKB1 is activated by protein kinase A (PKA) and Par-1, and is required for follicle cell polarity (Martin and St Johnston, 2003; Haack et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: A global reduction of the function of Egfr or of the downstream EGFR pathway modifiers brainiac or egghead disrupts the architecture of the follicle epithelium.
source: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling may also be important for follicle cell polarity because a global reduction of the function of Egfr or of the downstream EGFR pathway modifiers brainiac or egghead disrupts the architecture of the follicle epithelium; however cell-polarity markers were not investigated (Goode et al., 1992, 1996).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: In several different Drosophila and mammalian epithelia, the stem cells have a constricted or immature apical domain relative to the differentiated cell types in the tissue.
source: In several different Drosophila and mammalian epithelia, the stem cells have a constricted or immature apical domain relative to the differentiated cell types in the tissue (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Buske et al., 2011; Huo and Macara, 2014; Kronen et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published literature.

claim: Signals that regulate the development of cell polarity may play an important role in the segregation of epithelial stem cell and daughter cell fates.
source: Therefore, signals that regulate the development of cell polarity may play an important role in the segregation of epithelial stem cell and daughter cell fates.
evidence: Inferred from observations that stem cells have distinct polarity compared to differentiated cells.

claim: The relationship between cell polarity and differentiation in epithelial stem cell lineages is poorly understood.
source: However, the relationship between cell polarity and differentiation in epithelial stem cell lineages is poorly understood.
evidence: Statement about gaps in current knowledge.
